prose.title: The Long Haulers Got Paid to Take a Franchise Quarterback, and the Receivers Are Still Waiting
prose.dek: Brian Cross sent two future picks to HammerTime for Jalen Hurts and {{f.team.0006.trade_blind_bid_cash}} in blind-bid money, then spent just {{f.team.0006.faa_off_spend}} on offense at the Free Agent Auction, the least of anyone. He ranks {{f.team.0006.composite_rank|ord}} of {{f.league.teams}} with {{f.team.0006.studs_today}} studs, as many as anyone, but his receivers rank {{f.team.0006.wr_rank|ord}}.

paragraphs: The offense is genuinely strong at the top. Jalen Hurts grades High-end QB1 with Trevor Lawrence at Low-end QB1 in the superflex, which not every team in this format can say — two quarterbacks who are both actually good — and the room ranks {{f.team.0006.qb_rank|ord}}. The backfield ranks {{f.team.0006.rb_rank|ord}} on Najee Harris at High-end RB1 and Derrick Henry at Mid RB1. Tyler Warren is a High-end TE1 and tight end ranks {{f.team.0006.te_rank|ord}}.

Then the receivers, ranked {{f.team.0006.wr_rank|ord}} of {{f.league.teams}}, and the main flaw here. A.J. Brown grades Mid WR1 and Quentin Johnston Low-end WR4, and after those two the offensive flexes hold Jordan Mason, a Replacement-level RB, and Josh Downs, a Replacement-level WR.
Maxx Crosby and Brian Burns lead the defense, which is where most of his auction money went.

Composite {{f.team.0006.composite_rank|ord}} of {{f.league.teams}}, {{f.team.0006.studs_today}} studs, {{f.team.0006.holes_today}} holes. This is a top-heavy roster in the good sense: studs at both quarterback spots, both running back spots, the first receiver spot and tight end, and the gaps at the second receiver spot and in both offensive flexes.

April found him with {{f.team.0006.active_roster_opening}} active players, {{f.team.0006.cap_opening}} already committed and {{f.team.0006.studs_opening}} studs in place, a stud count only C-Town Chivalry and Sex Manther beat. The {{f.team.0006.holes_opening}} holes were the second back, the second receiver and both flexes. He did not begin the offseason rebuilding. He began it with a good team and a plan.

By the auction lock he was at {{f.team.0006.active_roster_preauction}} active with {{f.team.0006.cap_preauction}} committed, and the lineup had changed in one place: Quentin Johnston, a Low-end WR4, took the second receiver spot, pushing Josh Downs into a flex and Tre Tucker out. At that grade Johnston is still a hole, so the holes stayed at {{f.team.0006.holes_opening}} and the offense barely moved.

The auction filled him to {{f.team.0006.active_roster_current}} active players, the roster maximum of {{f.league.roster_max_at_auction}} at the time, and {{f.team.0006.roster_total_postauction}} in all once taxi and reserve are counted. On offense it changed one name: George Holani replaced Woody Marks in the second flex, one Replacement-level RB for another, which is why his starting offense came out barely better and the holes still numbered {{f.team.0006.holes_postauction}}. The auction was not about offense.

Since then the lineup has kept moving. Najee Harris, a High-end RB1, has stepped in at running back, pushing Jordan Mason into a flex and Holani to the bench, and the studs are up to {{f.team.0006.studs_today}} with holes down to {{f.team.0006.holes_today}}. He is the only owner whose lineup is measurably better now than it was when the auction closed.

At the Expired Rookie Auction he won {{f.team.0006.era_lots_won}} players for {{f.team.0006.era_spend}}, both at the league minimum: Tyjae Spears and Will Levis. That pool sells players whose rookie contracts ran out without earning a second one, and the most expensive man in it anywhere went for {{f.league.era_top_price}}. Spending the minimum twice is exactly the right way to treat it.

At the Free Agent Auction he won {{f.team.0006.faa_lots_won}} players for {{f.team.0006.faa_spend}}, one of the smallest budgets in the league, and {{f.team.0006.idp_auction_spend}} of it went on defenders: {{f.team.0006.idp_auction_share}} of everything he spent across both auctions, by a distance the largest defensive share of any owner.

Measured on offense alone, that auction barely registered. He spent {{f.team.0006.faa_off_spend}} on quarterbacks, backs, receivers and tight ends, the least of anyone, and for what that money bought he ranks {{f.team.0006.faa_off_rank|ord}} of {{f.league.teams}}, ahead of HammerTime, Pure Greatness and Cleon Ca$h but behind Gride. That grades only the few dollars he put into offense: the four owners who spent least there fill the bottom four places, and most of his money went to the other side of the ball.

His top buy of the summer was Maxx Crosby at {{f.team.0006.top_buy_price}}, against a league-high price elsewhere of {{f.league.faa_top_price}}, and the other defenders he bought came cheaper still. What the money never fixed was a receiver room ranked {{f.team.0006.wr_rank|ord}}: Jalen Nailor at the minimum was the only receiver he bought, and he was gone within the month.

t.0006.faa_value.title: Who got the most for his money

captions.t.0006.faa_value: Ranked by how much each owner's starting offense improved between the auction lock and the close, for every dollar he spent on quarterbacks, backs, receivers and tight ends at the Free Agent Auction.

paragraphs: {{f.team.0006.contracts_count}} contract moves, {{f.team.0006.trades_count}} trades and {{f.team.0006.roster_removals_total}} roster removals. Only Real Deal Creel cleared more players off a roster this summer.

The trade of his year, and arguably of anybody's year, came on the ninth of April. He sent his own 2027 first and second to HammerTime and received Jalen Hurts and {{f.team.0006.trade_blind_bid_cash}} of blind-bid money. He acquired a High-end QB1 and was paid cash to do it. Two future picks is a real price and future firsts are not free, but a quarterback of that grade with money attached is the kind of deal most owners never get offered.
He then extended Hurts and restructured him the same day, which back-loaded the deal and cut this season's charge.

The pick work is aggressive. In May he sent five picks to Sex Manther for two, moving up rather than out, and Sex Manther turned that haul into five players. He swapped with Gride to land 2.05 and 2.10. He gave a 2027 third to Pure Greatness for Quentin Johnston, who is now his second receiver. In July he sent Isaiah Bond and a 2027 fourth to L.A. Looks for Jordan Battle, a top-twelve defensive back who now starts for him — a small deal that quietly worked.

The removals are relentless: {{f.team.0006.cuts_count}} contracts cut and {{f.team.0006.inyear_flyers}} bodies signed and discarded inside the same offseason. Most cost nothing, several were taxi players whose salary was never on the cap at all. Three carry penalties deferred to next season, totaling {{f.team.0006.cuts_penalty_2027_deferred}}, and Theo Johnson's cut leaves {{f.team.0006.cuts_penalty_unstamped}} with no charge year stamped on it. This season's charge so far is {{f.team.0006.cuts_penalty_2026}}, but that is still a pile of small bills waiting to land.

The rookie class is the one genuine disappointment. Fernando Mendoza at 1.03 sits in one of the strongest historical bands of the whole draft, and he grades Replacement-level QB on the bench behind two quarterbacks who are both better than him. Carson Beck at 3.04 came from a slot history says produces nothing. Of {{f.team.0006.rookie_picks_count}} picks, not one is currently a starter.

He is {{f.team.0006.division_rank|ord}} of {{f.team.0006.division_size}}, behind Pure Greatness and ahead of HammerTime, and he meets both of them several times this season, starting in the opening week. HammerTime is the team he got Hurts from, so every one of those games re-argues the trade, and right now he is winning that argument.

Strongest team in the league? No, {{f.team.0006.composite_rank|ord}} of {{f.league.teams}} — but he has as many studs as the top-ranked team does. Good offseason? Yes, and most of it is one trade: he acquired a High-end QB1 with cash attached, kept his bill for both auctions to {{f.team.0006.auction_spend}}, and is the only owner whose lineup has improved since the auction closed.

The biggest advantage is the core of the offense, with studs at both quarterback spots and both running back spots. The biggest weakness is receiver, ranked {{f.team.0006.wr_rank|ord}}, where the entire room is A.J. Brown and hope.

Which brings us to the caveat, and it is one game — {{f.league.wk_teams_final}} NFL teams had played when this was written. His three starters whose games are over banked {{f.team.0006.wk_points_final}} points; George Holani ran for a few more on the bench, where they count for nothing. A.J. Brown, by a distance the most expensive of those players, was outscored by Jason Myers, a kicker bought at the league minimum. That is one box score, not a verdict on Brown or on paying up for a receiver.
